title: Banking Basics
description: Checking, savings, debit cards and deposits: how a bank account actually works.
wolfLine: A bank is a den for your money. Pick a good one.

fdic-insurance.definition: US government protection for bank deposits: if an insured bank fails, you get your money back, up to $250,000 per person, per bank.
fdic-insurance.example: Your bank closes with $3,000 of yours inside. The FDIC pays you the $3,000.

direct-deposit.definition: Your pay sent electronically straight into your bank account, with no paper check.
direct-deposit.example: Your paycheck lands in checking every other Friday morning.

checking-account.definition: A bank account for everyday money: your pay lands there, and card payments and bills come out of it.
checking-account.example: Your paycheck arrives, then rent and groceries leave from the same account.

debit-card.definition: A card that spends money straight from your checking account.
debit-card.example: Tap it for a $30 shirt and $30 leaves your checking account right away.

atm.definition: A cash machine. Use your debit card and PIN to take out or deposit cash.
atm.example: Taking $60 out of the machine outside your bank.

deposit.definition: Money going into your account, like your pay, a check or cash.
deposit.example: Your $1,079.40 paycheck arriving is a deposit.

available-balance.definition: The money you can actually spend right now, after holds and pending payments.
available-balance.example: Your balance is $520, but a $400 check is on hold, so $120 is available.

pending-transaction.definition: A payment that’s started but hasn’t finished going through. The money is already promised.
pending-transaction.example: A $58 grocery charge from last night that hasn’t come off your balance yet.

credit-union.definition: A bank-like institution owned by its members, which often means lower fees and better rates.
credit-union.example: A credit union for teachers in your county.

online-bank.definition: A bank with no branches: everything happens in an app or website, which often means fewer fees.
online-bank.example: An app-only bank with no monthly fee and a higher savings rate.

two-factor-authentication.definition: Logging in with two things: your password plus a code sent to your phone.
two-factor-authentication.example: You type your password, then a 6-digit code your bank texts you.

lessons.title: Why Use a Bank?
lessons.summary: Safer than a mattress, and it does work for you.

steps.title: Your money’s home base
steps.body:
A bank keeps your money safe, lets you pay bills and spend with a card, and gives your employer somewhere to send your pay.

Cash at home can be lost, stolen or burned, and nobody pays it back. Money in an insured bank is protected.

steps.context: Most US bank accounts have [[FDIC insurance]]: if the bank fails, the government pays you back, up to **$250,000** per person, per bank.
steps.prompt: Your bank goes out of business. You had $3,000 in your account. What happens?
steps.explain: Up to $250,000 per person, per bank, is covered. Your $3,000 is safe.

steps.prompt: Cash hidden at home is protected by FDIC insurance.
steps.explain: FDIC insurance only covers money in an insured bank.

steps.context: With [[direct deposit]], your employer sends your pay straight into your account. No paper check needed.
steps.prompt: What’s the main benefit of direct deposit?
choices: Your pay arrives on its own, often faster
steps.explain: No paper check to lose, no trip to the bank, and often the money arrives sooner.

steps.prompt: Which is the safest place for $2,000 of savings?
steps.explain: Insured, protected, and it can earn a little interest.

steps.prompt: If your bank fails, FDIC insurance covers up to ___ per person, per bank.
steps.explain: $250,000. More than enough for most people.

lessons.title: Checking vs. Savings
lessons.summary: One account for spending, one for keeping.

steps.context: A [[checking account]] is for everyday money: your pay lands there, and bills and card payments come out of it.
steps.prompt: What’s a checking account for?
choices: Money you won’t touch for years
steps.explain: Checking is where money comes and goes.

steps.context: A [[savings account]] is for money you’re keeping, not spending. It usually pays you a little [[interest]]: extra money for leaving it there.
steps.prompt: Where should next year’s holiday money live?
choices: In checking with the rent money
steps.explain: Separate and growing, so you don’t spend it by accident.

steps.prompt: Checking or savings? Sort them.
items: Paying rent
Emergency money
Buying groceries with your card
Money for a car in two years
Your paycheck landing
Holiday fund

steps.prompt: Keeping savings in a separate account makes you less likely to spend it by accident.
steps.explain: Out of sight of your card, out of reach of your impulses.

steps.context: Savings interest is shown as a yearly percentage. 1% of $1,000 is $10 a year.
steps.prompt: Your savings account pays 2% a year. How much interest does $1,500 earn in a year?
Why not keep everything in savings?
choices: Savings accounts aren’t built for daily card payments and bills
Savings accounts are illegal for young people
steps.explain: Many savings accounts limit withdrawals. Checking handles the daily traffic.

steps.prompt: You get paid. What’s a simple setup?
choices: Pay lands in checking, and a set amount moves to savings
steps.explain: Spend from one account, build in the other.

lessons.title: Opening an Account
lessons.summary: What to bring, what to ask, what to skip.

steps.title: What you’ll need
steps.body:
To open an account you usually need a photo ID, your Social Security number, an address, and sometimes a small first deposit.

Under 18? You’ll usually need a parent or guardian on the account with you.

steps.prompt: Which do you usually need to open a bank account?
choices: A photo ID and your Social Security number
steps.explain: Banks have to check who you are. ID and Social Security number do that.

steps.prompt: Before you sign up, what’s the most important thing to ask?
choices: What fees could I be charged, and how do I avoid them?
What color is the debit card?
steps.explain: Fees are where a “free” account stops being free.

steps.prompt: Put opening an account in order.
items: Compare a few banks or credit unions
Check the fees and the insurance
Apply with your ID and Social Security number
Make your first deposit and set up direct deposit
steps.explain: Shop, check, apply, fund.

steps.prompt: A bank asking for your Social Security number when you open an account is normal.
steps.explain: Banks are required to confirm who you are. Just never give it to someone who contacts you out of the blue.

steps.prompt: The banker offers a credit card, an overdraft plan and a paid “account protection” add-on. What do you do?
choices: Say no for now and open just the basic accounts
steps.explain: Start simple. You can always add things later once you understand them.

lessons.title: Debit Cards & ATMs
lessons.summary: Spending your own money, one tap at a time.

steps.context: A [[debit card]] spends money straight from your checking account. Tap it, and the money leaves.
steps.prompt: You buy a $30 shirt with your debit card. Where does the money come from?
choices: The bank lends it to you
steps.explain: Straight out of checking, right away.

steps.context: An [[ATM]] is a cash machine. Your debit card and PIN (a secret 4-digit code) let you take out cash.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a mistake?
choices: Writing your PIN on the back of your card
Covering the keypad as you type your PIN
steps.explain: Lose the card and you’ve handed over the code too.

steps.context: ATMs outside your bank’s network often charge a fee, and your own bank may charge one too.
steps.prompt: The ATM charges $3.50 and your own bank adds $2.50. What does it cost to take out $40?
steps.explain: $3.50 + $2.50 = $6 to get $40. That’s 15% of the cash.

steps.prompt: You do that twice a week for a year, 104 times. What do the fees add up to?
With a debit card, you can never spend more than what’s in your account.
steps.explain: Some banks let the payment through anyway and charge a fee for it. You’ll meet that trap in the next unit.

steps.prompt: Your debit card is lost. First move?
choices: Lock or report it in your bank app right away
Wait a week to see if it turns up
Keep using the card number online
steps.explain: Lock it now. You can unlock it if it turns up in your jacket.

steps.prompt: A debit card takes money from your ___ account.
steps.explain: Checking. That’s what it’s linked to.

lessons.title: Money In: Deposits & Holds
lessons.summary: Why your balance and your spendable money can differ.

steps.context: A [[deposit]] is money going into your account: your pay, a check, cash at the counter.
steps.prompt: Which of these is a deposit?
steps.explain: Money in is a deposit. The other two are money out.

steps.context: When you deposit a check, the bank may hold it for a day or two before you can spend it. Your [[available balance]] is what you can spend right now.
steps.prompt: You deposit a $400 check this morning. Your account shows $520, but your available balance is $120. Why?
steps.explain: $520 − $400 on hold = $120 you can use right now.

steps.prompt: Your balance is $860. A $250 check you deposited is still on hold. What’s your available balance?
You should spend based on your available balance, not your total balance.
steps.explain: The available balance is the real number.

steps.prompt: You deposited a check by photographing it in your bank app. What should you do with the paper check?
choices: Keep it safe for a couple of weeks, then destroy it
Deposit it again at the branch
Hand it back to the person who wrote it
steps.explain: Keep it until the deposit fully clears. Depositing it twice causes real trouble.

steps.prompt: Put a phone check deposit in order.
items: Sign the back of the check
Photograph it in your bank app
Wait for the hold to clear
Spend the money
steps.explain: Sign, snap, wait, spend.

lessons.title: Alex Checks the Balance
lessons.summary: A balance can look bigger than it really is.

story.title: Plenty of money. Or not?
story.body:
On Friday morning Alex’s banking app shows a balance of **$412**. Alex wants to buy a concert ticket.

What Alex doesn’t notice: three [[pending transactions|pending-transaction]] haven’t finished going through. A **$58** grocery run, **$24** of gas and **$9** for a streaming service. Pending means the money is already promised, even though the balance hasn’t dropped yet.

The concert ticket costs **$340**.

steps.prompt: Add up the three pending transactions.
How much does Alex really have once they go through?
Can Alex afford the $340 ticket today?
choices: No, there’s only $321 once the pending payments clear
why: The balance is out of date by $91.
They count. The money is already promised.
steps.explain: The balance hasn’t caught up with what’s already been spent.

steps.prompt: How much is Alex short?
Pending transactions can take a day or two to fully go through.
steps.explain: That’s why the balance lags behind.

steps.prompt: Which habit would have saved Alex?
choices: Checking pending transactions before a big purchase
steps.explain: Balance minus pending is what you really have.

lessons.title: Banks, Credit Unions & Online Banks
lessons.summary: Three kinds of homes for your money. Compare them.

steps.context: A [[credit union]] is like a bank, but owned by its members. Profits come back as lower fees and better rates.
steps.prompt: Who owns a credit union?
steps.explain: Members own it, so profits go back to them.

steps.context: An [[online bank]] has no branches. Lower costs often mean fewer fees and better interest on savings.
steps.prompt: What’s the usual trade-off with an online bank?
steps.explain: Insured online banks are just as protected. You just can’t visit one.

steps.context: Compare accounts on what **you** would pay, based on how you actually bank.

docs.title: City Bank Everyday
docs.subtitle: Checking account
docs.note: Monthly fee waived if you keep $1,500 or more in the account.

docs.title: Cloud Checking
docs.subtitle: Online bank checking
docs.note: No branches. Everything happens in the app.

steps.prompt: You usually keep about $600 in checking. Which account costs you less?
steps.explain: With $600 you’d never reach City Bank’s $1,500 waiver, so you’d pay $12 every month.

docs.title: City Bank Everyday
docs.subtitle: Checking account
docs.note: Monthly fee waived if you keep $1,500 or more in the account.

docs.title: Cloud Checking
docs.subtitle: Online bank checking
docs.note: No branches. Everything happens in the app.

steps.prompt: With $600 in the account, what would City Bank’s monthly fee cost you over a year?
Online banks and credit unions can’t be insured.
steps.explain: Insured online banks have FDIC insurance. Credit unions have the same kind of cover through the NCUA.

steps.prompt: Which is it?
items: Owned by investors who want a profit
Owned by its members
No branches, all in an app
You join through where you live or work
Lower fees because there are no branches
Big branch network across the country

lessons.title: Keep Your Account Safe
lessons.summary: Passwords, codes and alerts: lock the den.

steps.context: Most account break-ins start with a stolen password, not a bank robbery.
steps.prompt: Which password is strongest?
choices: A long phrase only you know, used nowhere else
The same password you use everywhere
steps.explain: Long, unique, and not guessable from your social media.

steps.context: [[Two-factor authentication]] means logging in takes two things: your password **and** a code sent to your phone.
steps.prompt: Someone steals your password. With two-factor on, what stops them?
choices: They don’t have the code from your phone
steps.explain: Without your phone, the password alone isn’t enough.

steps.prompt: Your bank may text you to ask for your full password or PIN.
steps.explain: Banks never ask for your PIN or password by text, email or phone. Anyone who does is a scammer.

steps.context: Turn on alerts. Your bank can message you for every purchase, low balances and big withdrawals.
steps.prompt: You get an alert for a $240 purchase you didn’t make. First move?
choices: Lock your card and call the bank on the number printed on your card
Reply to the text with your details
Wait and see if more charges appear
steps.explain: Use a number you trust, never one from the message.

steps.prompt: A strange charge shows up. Put your response in order.
items: Lock your card in the app
Call the bank on the number on your card
Report the charge as fraud
Change your password
steps.explain: Stop the bleeding, tell the bank, then lock things down.

steps.prompt: Logging into your bank on public café Wi-Fi is as safe as at home.
steps.explain: Public Wi-Fi can be watched. Use your phone’s data or a network you trust.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Banking
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: Which account should your paycheck land in?
steps.explain: Checking, then move your saving out.

steps.prompt: Your balance is $730, with pending charges of $85 and $40. How much is available to spend?
FDIC insurance covers up to $250,000 per person, per bank.
steps.explain: That’s the limit.

steps.prompt: A text says “Your account is locked. Reply with your PIN.” What is it?
steps.explain: Banks never ask for your PIN. Delete it.
